notes.title: Concept - Benchmark Taxonomy
notes.scope: The map of what LLM benchmarks measure and how they score, organized by capability axis (knowledge, reasoning, math, code, instruction-following, long-context, multilingual, safety) crossed with scoring paradigm (closed-form log-likelihood, generation-plus-parse, execution-based, model-judged, human-preference). IN: the orienting framework and one canonical exemplar per cell. OUT: deep flaws of individual benchmarks (link to the Breakdown notes), statistical methodology (link to Statistical Rigor), and domain-specific agent/RAG evals (owned by 10/11).
key_points: Two axes: WHAT is measured vs HOW it is scored. Scoring paradigms determine reproducibility more than the questions do.

Exemplars per cell: MMLU/GPQA (knowledge/reasoning MCQ, log-likelihood), GSM8K/MATH/AIME (math, generate+parse), HumanEval/MBPP/LiveCodeBench/SWE-bench (code, execution-based pass@k), IFEval (programmatic instruction checks), MT-Bench/AlpacaEval/Arena-Hard (LLM-judged), Chatbot Arena (human Elo), RULER/needle-in-haystack (long context), MMMU (multimodal)
Metric families: accuracy/exact-match, F1, pass@k, BLEU/ROUGE (largely dead for generation quality), Elo/Bradley-Terry, win-rate
Benchmark lifecycle: benchmarks saturate and die. GLUE -> SuperGLUE -> saturated; GSM8K ~95%+ by 2024; MMLU ~88-90 plateauing -> MMLU-Pro, GPQA, Humanity's Last Exam replace them
Static-public vs contamination-prone vs live/private: the axis that increasingly matters most (as of 2026)
Multiple-choice vs open-generation is not a cosmetic difference: MCQ measures recognition and is confounded by option position; generation measures production but needs parsing or a judge
Random and human baselines are part of a benchmark's identity (MMLU random 25%, expert ~89.8%); a score is meaningless without them
links: Concept - Statistical Rigor in Model Evaluation

notes.title: Concept - Goodhart's Law in Model Evaluation
notes.scope: How and why a benchmark stops measuring the capability it was meant to proxy once labs optimize toward it. IN: the mechanism of measure-target decoupling in ML, the taxonomy of Goodhart failure modes, and the concrete decoupling evidence. OUT: reward hacking as an RL training pathology (owned by 06, link out) and contamination as one specific decoupling vector (link to Benchmark Contamination).
key_points: Strathern's phrasing 'when a measure becomes a target it ceases to be a good measure'; original Goodhart from 1975 monetary policy
Mechanism: optimizing to a benchmark (training on near-distribution data, tuning data mix or architecture to a leaderboard) raises the number while decoupling it from the latent capability it proxied

Decoupling evidence: GSM1k (Zhang et al. 2024) rebuilt GSM8K-style problems fresh; several model families dropped 8-13% (worst: some Mistral/Phi checkpoints), frontier models robust -> quantifies overfit
Manheim & Garrabrant taxonomy: regressional, extremal, causal, adversarial Goodhart -- each a different failure of the proxy
Leaderboard hillclimbing: AlpacaEval win-rate gamed by output length until length-controlled version shipped; MT-Bench style-gaming
Reward hacking (06) is the training-time cousin; contamination is the data-time cousin; this note owns the general principle
Defenses: private/held-out sets, rotating and templated benchmarks (GSM-Symbolic), measuring under distribution shift, tracking benchmark-vs-real-task correlation over time

notes.title: Concept - LLM-as-Judge
notes.scope: Using a strong LLM to score or rank model outputs in place of humans. IN: the pointwise/pairwise/reference-guided mechanics, the named systematic biases with measured magnitudes, and the standard debiasing moves. OUT: how you validate that a judge is trustworthy (link to Meta-Evaluation of LLM Judges), the aggregated pitfall catalogue (link to Gotchas - LLM-as-Judge Evaluations), and reward models for RLHF (owned by 06).
key_points: Three modes: pointwise (score 1-10), pairwise (A vs B, most reliable), reference-guided (grade against a gold answer). Pairwise + Bradley-Terry aggregation is the robust default
Position bias: judges systematically prefer the first (or a fixed) position; Zheng et al. 2023 (MT-Bench/Chatbot Arena judge paper) measured it and introduced swap-and-average / consistency scoring
Verbosity/length bias: longer answers win regardless of quality -> AlpacaEval 2.0 introduced length-controlled win-rate to neutralize it
Self-preference / self-enhancement bias: models rate their own family's outputs higher (Panickssery et al. 2024 tie it to the model recognizing its own generation style)
Calibration: GPT-4-class judges reach ~80% agreement with humans on MT-Bench, comparable to human-human ~81%, but collapse on hard reasoning where a fluent-but-wrong answer fools them
Systems: MT-Bench, AlpacaEval 2.0, Arena-Hard-Auto, G-Eval (probability-weighted scoring), Prometheus (open judge model), JudgeLM
Standard mitigations: position swapping, chain-of-thought before verdict, rubric and reference anchoring, few-shot exemplars, ensemble/panel of judges, cross-family judge to dodge self-preference
Hard failure: judge weaker than the judged; gameable by adversarial phrasing and prompt injection inside the candidate output

notes.title: Concept - Benchmark Contamination
notes.scope: Test data (or near-duplicates of it) leaking into pretraining or fine-tuning corpora, inflating scores without real capability. IN: the leakage vectors, canary-string discipline, effect sizes, and a preview of detection. OUT: the detection algorithms in depth (link to Membership Inference for Contamination Detection) and corpus deduplication mechanics (owned by 05).
key_points: Vectors: direct inclusion (benchmark mirrored on GitHub/HuggingFace and scraped), indirect (solutions in blogs, Stack Overflow, textbooks), synthetic-data leakage (teacher trained on the test), and outright eval-on-train
Canary strings: BIG-bench embeds a unique GUID; benchmark authors insert canaries so anyone can check whether a model reproduces them -- respecting the canary is a norm, not enforcement

Rephrasing defeats naive decontamination: Yang et al. 2023 'Rethinking Benchmark and Contamination with Rephrased Samples' -- a 13B model trained on paraphrased/translated test items reaches GPT-4-level scores while passing n-gram decontamination
Effect sizes: contamination can add tens of points on affected benchmarks; the GPT-4 technical report disclosed contamination on several benchmarks and reported decontaminated splits
Temporal signal: models score higher on problems dated before their training cutoff -- the basis for LiveCodeBench-style date-windowing

Detection preview: exact n-gram overlap (weak), embedding/paraphrase overlap (harder), min-k% probability, guided-prompting completion tests, Oren et al. 2023 exchangeability test on canonical benchmark ordering
Practitioner reality: perfect decontamination is impossible at web scale; release-date discipline, canaries, and private/live benchmarks are the durable defenses
links: Concept - Membership Inference for Contamination Detection

notes.title: Concept - Capability versus Propensity
notes.scope: The distinction between what a model CAN do under best elicitation (capability) and what it TENDS to do by default (propensity), and why conflating them wrecks eval conclusions. IN: the elicitation gap, why 'the model can't do X' is usually an elicitation failure, and the eval-design implications. OUT: safety/dangerous-capability eval framing (owned by 14) and the CoT mechanism itself (owned by 09).
key_points: Capability = best-case performance under maximal elicitation (few-shot, CoT, tools, fine-tuning, best-of-n); propensity = default behavior in natural conditions. They require opposite eval setups
Elicitation gap is large: chain-of-thought lifts GSM8K from ~15% to ~55% on the same PaLM weights (Wei et al. 2022) -- identical model, different measured capability
'The model can't do X' is usually an elicitation failure, not a capability ceiling; negative results need a max-elicitation attempt before they count
Sandbagging: a model (or a fine-tune) can deliberately underperform; Greenblatt et al. password-locked models demonstrate hidden capability that standard evals miss

Safety consequence: dangerous-capability evals must elicit the ceiling (even fine-tune to elicit), while alignment/propensity evals must observe default behavior -- using the wrong frame under- or over-states risk
pass@k leans toward capability (retries), pass@1 leans toward deployment propensity; reporting one as the other is a common inflation
Elicitation as an active research area (Anthropic and DeepMind dangerous-capability evaluations, 2023-2025)
links: Concept - Chain-of-Thought and Why It Works

notes.title: Concept - Human Evaluation Methodology
notes.scope: How to run human evaluation of model outputs so the numbers mean something. IN: study designs, inter-annotator agreement statistics, reliability failure modes, and preference aggregation. OUT: automating this with a model (link to LLM-as-Judge), preference collection for RLHF training (owned by 06), and the significance tests themselves (link to Statistical Rigor).
key_points: Designs: pairwise preference (A/B, lowest cognitive load, most reliable), Likert/rubric scoring, best-of-n ranking, structured error annotation. Pairwise beats absolute scoring for consistency

Inter-annotator agreement: Cohen's kappa (2 raters), Fleiss' kappa (n raters, fixed items), Krippendorff's alpha (any scale, handles missing data); raw agreement misleads because it ignores chance -- kappa 0.6-0.8 = substantial
Reliability failures: annotator drift and fatigue, low-effort/spam workers (catch with gold-standard attention checks), ambiguous guidelines, and cultural/demographic bias in preferences
Rater-quality-aware aggregation: Dawid-Skene and MACE weight annotators by estimated reliability instead of naive majority vote; Bradley-Terry/Elo for pairwise battles
Expert vs crowd: MMLU-grade knowledge needs experts; helpfulness/preference can use crowd; mismatched pool is a silent error (the InstructGPT paper used trained contractors, not raw crowd)
Scale example: Chatbot Arena is crowdsourced human eval at >2M votes; the tradeoff is uncontrolled prompt distribution and self-selected raters
Power and cost: number of annotations needed to detect a given effect; human eval runs ~$0.5-5/sample and days, versus seconds and sub-cent for an LLM judge

notes.title: Concept - Statistical Rigor in Model Evaluation
notes.scope: Treating a benchmark score as a random variable and comparing models with proper uncertainty. IN: confidence intervals for accuracy, paired significance testing, variance sources, multiple-comparison correction, and power/sample-size reasoning. OUT: the runnable bootstrap (link to Snippet - Paired Bootstrap) and inter-annotator agreement stats (link to Human Evaluation Methodology).
key_points: The core sin: single-number accuracy with no CI, then declaring model A > B on a fraction-of-a-point gap that is inside the noise
CIs for proportions: Wald is wrong at the tails; use Wilson or Clopper-Pearson. Rule of thumb width ~1.96*sqrt(p(1-p)/n); at 50% on a 1000-item benchmark that is roughly +/-3.1 points
Small benchmarks have brutal CIs: GPQA-Diamond ~198 items, AIME ~30 items/year -- on AIME a single question is 3.3%, so most reported AIME gaps are not significant

Paired testing is the free lunch: both models answer the same items, so use McNemar's test (paired binary), paired bootstrap, or permutation tests -- far more power than comparing two independent CIs (whose marginal intervals can overlap while the difference is significant)
Variance beyond sampling: prompt template, few-shot choice and order, decoding seed, and judge model all inject variance; report across seeds/formats (Miller 2024 'Adding Error Bars to Evals')
Multiple comparisons: an N-model leaderboard guarantees someone wins by chance; apply Bonferroni or false-discovery control before crowning a winner
Hierarchical structure: MMLU subjects and multi-item-per-doc benchmarks violate independence -> use clustered/hierarchical bootstrap, not item-level iid
links: Snippet - Paired Bootstrap for Model Comparison

notes.title: Breakdown - MMLU
notes.scope: The Massive Multitask Language Understanding benchmark: what it is, how it is actually scored, its documented label errors, and its successors. IN: the construction, the scoring-implementation variance, the error-rate findings, and the MMLU-Pro/Redux lineage. OUT: the token-level scoring arcana (link to Answer Scoring and Normalization and Multiple-Choice Symbol Binding) and general contamination mechanics (link to Benchmark Contamination).
key_points: Hendrycks et al. 2021: 57 subjects, ~14k test MCQs, 4 options each, spanning STEM/humanities/professional exams; random baseline 25%, human expert ~89.8%
Became THE knowledge benchmark; frontier reached ~86-90% by 2024 and plateaued -> saturation drove replacements

Scoring is under-specified and implementations disagree: log-likelihood of the letter token vs full answer text, 0-shot vs 5-shot, chat template or not -- HELM, lm-eval-harness, and the original code produce different numbers for the same model (the 2023 Open LLM Leaderboard MMLU discrepancy)

Label quality: MMLU-Redux (Gema et al. 2024) re-annotated a sample and found ~6.5% of questions have errors overall, with some subjects (e.g. virology) exceeding 50% -- wrong ground truth caps achievable accuracy
Contamination: MMLU is all over the web and in most pretraining corpora; treat public MMLU as partly memorized
Successors: MMLU-Pro (10 options, harder distractors, reasoning-heavy, TIGER-Lab 2024), MMLU-Redux (cleaned labels), GPQA (Google-proof, contamination-resistant)
What to steal: subject breadth and cheapness; but clean your labels, fix the scoring method, and report per-subject CIs before trusting a delta

notes.title: Playbook - Building a Production Eval Suite
notes.scope: Eval-driven development for a shipped LLM product: building the offline+online suite that catches regressions before users do. IN: the end-to-end procedure from failure-case collection to CI gating and online A/B. OUT: harness internals (link to Designing an Eval Harness) and general observability/tracing plumbing (owned by 16).
key_points: Step 1: mine real production failures and edge cases into a versioned golden set; ~100-300 well-chosen, sliced-by-segment cases beat 10k noisy ones
Step 2: define per-capability metrics (task success, format/schema compliance, safety, latency, cost) rather than one blended score

Step 3: pick the cheapest sufficient grader per metric -- exact/regex, code execution, LLM-judge with a pinned rubric, human spot-check -- and pin the judge model snapshot so a silent provider upgrade cannot move your scores
Step 4: wire into CI so a regression blocks deploy; replay sampled production traffic offline; then run online A/B with guardrail metrics
Tooling: OpenAI Evals, promptfoo, Braintrust, LangSmith, UK AISI Inspect, DeepEval
Failure modes: your own team contaminating the eval set, judge-version drift, overfitting to the golden set (Goodhart), and flaky LLM-judge nondeterminism
Verification: inject a known-bad prompt or a past regression and confirm the suite actually fails -- an eval that never goes red is decorative

notes.title: Decision - Choosing an Evaluation Method
notes.scope: Picking the right evaluation method for a given question: execution-based, static closed-form, LLM-as-judge, human eval, or online A/B. IN: the decision flow, the tradeoff matrix with cost/latency/reliability numbers, and the edge cases that flip the default. OUT: how to actually run each method (link to the Playbook and Human Evaluation Methodology notes).
key_points: Decision flow: programmatic ground truth exists? -> exact-match or execution. Open-ended quality? -> LLM-judge (fast iteration) or human (high stakes). Need real-world impact? -> online A/B. Verifiable but generative? -> pass@k execution
Default for the 80% case: execution-based where a verifier exists; LLM-judge for open-ended dev-loop iteration; escalate to human for launch/safety-critical calls

Tradeoff matrix (per sample): execution ~free & deterministic but only for verifiable tasks; LLM-judge ~$0.001-0.01 and seconds but biased/gameable; human ~$0.5-5 and days but the gold reference; online A/B measures real impact but needs traffic and has confounders
Reliability ranking for correlation with true quality: human ~ execution > calibrated LLM-judge > naive LLM-judge >> lexical overlap (BLEU/ROUGE, effectively dead for quality)

Flip factors: LLM-judge collapses on hard reasoning and adversarial phrasing; execution false-positives on weak test suites; human needed when subtlety or safety dominates; A/B confounded by novelty and segment mix
Combine, don't choose once: cheap judge for CI gating, human audit on a sampled slice, online A/B as the final arbiter

notes.title: Checklist - Trusting a Benchmark Number
notes.scope: The pre-flight verification to run before believing a leaderboard cell, a paper's headline score, or a vendor launch chart. IN: atomic checks across reproducibility, contamination, statistics, apples-to-apples comparability, and gaming, each tied to a real incident. OUT: the full statistical machinery (link to Statistical Rigor) and the scoring-method arcana (link to Answer Scoring and Normalization).
key_points: Reproducibility group: is the harness named and version-pinned, the prompt template and shot count reported, and the scoring method (log-likelihood vs generation, acc vs acc_norm) stated?
Contamination group: model training cutoff vs benchmark release date checked, decontamination reported, canary respected?
Statistics group: is n reported, are CIs present, is the claimed gap larger than the CI, was a paired test used across seeds/formats?
Apples-to-apples group: same shots, same subset/version, same answer-parsing across all compared models, correct chat template applied to instruct models?
Judge/human group: judge model and position-debiasing disclosed; inter-annotator agreement reported for human results?
Gaming group: any sign of training on the train split, tuning to the leaderboard, or a length/format/style confound?
Why-these-items section ties each to an incident: the 2023 Open LLM Leaderboard MMLU discrepancy, Reflection-70B, AlpacaEval length gaming, GSM1k drops
links: Concept - Statistical Rigor in Model Evaluation
Deep Dive - Designing an Eval Harness

notes.title: Deep Dive - Designing an Eval Harness
notes.scope: How an evaluation harness turns a dataset and a model into a comparable number, and the design decisions that make or break reproducibility. IN: the full request-to-report pipeline, the reference systems, the load-bearing configuration choices, and the reproducibility crisis. OUT: the deepest scoring/normalization arcana (link to Answer Scoring and Normalization) and prompt-format variance (link to Prompt Format Sensitivity).
key_points: Pipeline: load dataset -> doc_to_text/doc_to_target formatting -> apply few-shot and chat template -> issue request (loglikelihood, loglikelihood_rolling, or generate_until) -> filter/extract answer -> score -> aggregate -> report. Include a Mermaid/ASCII diagram of this flow

Reference systems: EleutherAI lm-evaluation-harness (de facto standard, powers the Open LLM Leaderboard, YAML task specs), Stanford HELM (scenario x metric matrix, holistic), OpenAI Evals, UK AISI Inspect (tool-use/agent evals), BigCode evaluation harness

Load-bearing decisions: log-likelihood vs generation; answer normalization (acc vs acc_norm, byte-length); few-shot sampling (fixed seed vs random); chat-template application (running an instruct model without its template silently tanks it by 10-20 points); stop sequences; target delimiter and leading-space handling
Evolution: ad-hoc per-paper scripts -> lm-eval-harness (Gao et al.) standardizing tasks -> HELM's holistic matrix -> Inspect for agentic/tool evals as benchmarks moved to multi-step tasks

Reproducibility crisis: the same benchmark under different harnesses yields materially different numbers -- documented for MMLU across HELM/lm-eval/original code; a leaderboard is only self-consistent, not cross-comparable

Failure modes: wrong or missing chat template, answer-parsing regex that misses valid formats, generation truncated below CoT length, batch-size/padding nondeterminism, tokenizer leading-space logprob quirks
Design principle: pin everything (harness version, template, shots, scoring, seed) and treat any unpinned axis as a source of silent, unreproducible variance

notes.title: Breakdown - Chatbot Arena
notes.scope: The LMArena (formerly LMSYS Chatbot Arena) crowdsourced pairwise-battle leaderboard: how anonymous head-to-head votes become a Bradley-Terry rating with confidence intervals, and the style/length confounds and governance controversies that complicate it. IN: the rating mechanics, the clever design choices, the confounds, and the 2025 governance critique. OUT: the Bradley-Terry math as a general tool for preference learning (link to Reward Models) and human-eval methodology generally (link to Human Evaluation Methodology).
key_points: What: users chat with two anonymized models side-by-side and vote a winner; >2-3M votes accumulated by 2024-25; ratings via online updates then a Bradley-Terry MLE with bootstrap CIs (Chiang et al. 2024)

Rating math: Bradley-Terry models P(A beats B) = sigma(beta_A - beta_B); fit betas by maximum likelihood over all pairwise outcomes; report bootstrap confidence intervals so near-tied models share a rank band
Clever parts: real-world prompt distribution from actual users, hard to contaminate because prompts are fresh and private, and category slicing (coding, hard prompts, longer queries, multi-turn)

Style and length confound: longer, markdown-formatted, confident answers win independent of correctness -- LMArena shipped a 'Style Control' regression (2024) that decomposes length/formatting from substance and reorders the board
Other biases: self-selected raters and prompts, ties handling, non-transitivity of pairwise preferences, and possible gaming by fingerprinting a target model's style
2025 governance critique: 'The Leaderboard Illusion' (Singh et al. 2025) alleges private multi-variant testing, selective score disclosure, and data-access asymmetry favoring large labs
What to steal: pairwise + Bradley-Terry + bootstrap CIs is the right template for preference leaderboards -- but you must control for style or you are ranking verbosity
links: Concept - Statistical Rigor in Model Evaluation

notes.title: Breakdown - SWE-bench
notes.scope: The SWE-bench execution-based coding benchmark: resolve real GitHub issues by producing a patch that passes hidden tests. IN: the construction, the Verified/Lite subsets, why the original set was partly broken, the score trajectory, and the contamination/leakage angle. OUT: the agent scaffolds that actually solve the tasks (owned by 10) and general pass@k metric theory (link to Pass@k and Sampling-Based Evaluation).
key_points: Jimenez et al. 2023: ~2294 real issue+PR pairs from 12 popular Python repos; the model gets the repo at the base commit plus the issue text and must emit a patch; graded by running fail-to-pass and pass-to-pass test suites -- execution ground truth, no judge

Subsets: SWE-bench Lite (300 tasks), and SWE-bench Verified (500 tasks human-validated by OpenAI, Aug 2024) created because a large fraction of original tasks were underspecified, had broken/flaky tests, or were effectively unsolvable from the issue alone

Score trajectory: from ~2% (2023) to 60-70%+ (2025-26 on Verified) -- most of the gain came from agent scaffolding and better base models, a caution that the benchmark measures the scaffold+model system, not the model alone
Clever parts: real-world difficulty, execution as an unfakeable verifier, and pass-to-pass tests that catch regressions the patch might introduce

Flaws: solution leakage/contamination because the fixing PR is public and in pretraining corpora; weak test suites give false credit; environment-setup flakiness; localization can be gamed when the issue names the file
Contamination is cutoff-sensitive -- fresh/date-windowed variants (SWE-bench+, live coding sets) exist to counter it
What to steal: execution-based grading, a human-verified subset, and the fail-to-pass + pass-to-pass structure for regression-aware evaluation
links: Concept - Tool Use and Function Calling

notes.title: Concept - Pass@k and Sampling-Based Evaluation
notes.scope: Evaluating generative tasks that have verifiers by sampling multiple outputs and scoring the set. IN: the pass@k unbiased estimator, related sampling metrics, the capability-vs-deployment conflation, and verifier-quality pitfalls. OUT: reasoning-model training (owned by 06) and decoding-parameter mechanics (owned by 07, link out).
key_points: pass@k = probability that at least one of k samples passes the verifier; the naive fraction from exactly k samples is high-variance and biased upward
Codex/HumanEval unbiased estimator (Chen et al. 2021): draw n >= k samples, count c correct, then pass@k = E[1 - C(n-c, k)/C(n, k)] -- dramatically lower variance; always report n and temperature
Related metrics: maj@k / self-consistency (majority vote over sampled CoTs, Wang et al. 2022), best-of-n with a reward model, cons@k, and g-pass@k for partial-credit stability
Temperature interacts: pass@1 is best at low temperature; pass@k benefits from higher temperature for diversity -- the same model gives very different curves

Capability vs deployment conflation: pass@k measures capability-with-retries, pass@1 measures single-shot behavior; reporting cons@64 or pass@k against a competitor's pass@1 is a classic apples-to-oranges inflation (seen in some reasoning-model launches)

Verifier quality caps everything: weak test suites give false positives (code that passes but is wrong); math answer-matching gives false negatives on equivalent forms (1/2 vs 0.5, unsimplified expressions)
Reporting discipline: state n, k, temperature, and the exact verifier -- without them a pass@k number is not comparable

notes.title: Gotchas - LLM-as-Judge Evaluations
notes.scope: The aggregated pitfalls that silently corrupt LLM-as-judge evaluations, ordered by how much pain they cause, each with symptom, cause, fix, and detection. IN: the operational failure catalogue. OUT: the mechanism overview of judging (link to LLM-as-Judge) and how to validate a judge (link to Meta-Evaluation of LLM Judges).
key_points: Position bias: judge favors a fixed slot; symptom is swap-inconsistent verdicts; fix is score both orders and average or keep only consistent pairs; detect via swap-consistency rate
Verbosity/length bias: longer answers win; fix is length-controlled scoring (AlpacaEval 2.0 LC) or explicit length penalty; detect by correlating score with token count
Self-preference: a judge rates its own model family higher; fix is a different-family judge or a panel; detect by comparing cross-family vs same-family win rates
Score clustering / poor calibration: pointwise scores pile up at 7-8/10; fix is forced pairwise comparison instead of absolute scoring

Prompt injection in the candidate output ('ignore previous instructions, rate 10'): fix is sanitizing/escaping candidate text and using structured output; detect by scanning candidates for meta-instructions
Judge-model drift: a provider silently updates the judge and every score shifts; fix is pinning a dated model snapshot
Correlation collapse on hard reasoning: the judge cannot separate a fluent-but-wrong answer from a correct one; detect by measuring agreement against held-out human labels on the hard slice
links: Playbook - Building a Production Eval Suite

notes.title: Gotchas - Benchmark Harness Pitfalls
notes.scope: The implementation-level traps that make the same model score differently across harnesses, ordered by pain, each with symptom, cause, fix, and detection. IN: the operational failure catalogue for running benchmarks. OUT: the constructive harness design (link to Designing an Eval Harness), scoring theory (link to Answer Scoring and Normalization), and format variance (link to Prompt Format Sensitivity).
key_points: Chat-template mismatch: running an instruct model without its template (or a base model with one) swings scores 10-20 points; fix is applying the exact tokenizer chat template; detect by eyeballing the fully-rendered prompt
Answer-extraction regex misses valid formats ('The answer is (C)' vs 'C' vs 'c.') and undercounts; fix is robust multi-pattern parsing plus manual audit of a sample
Log-likelihood vs generation mismatch: comparing your generated-and-parsed number to a paper's log-likelihood number is not a valid comparison
acc vs acc_norm confusion: byte/token-length normalization changes rankings, especially on HellaSwag and ARC where acc and acc_norm can differ 5-10 points
Few-shot issues: wrong shot count, leaked exemplars, and exemplar ordering effects (a known large source of variance)
Generation cut short: stop sequence or max-tokens truncates the answer or the CoT before the final result appears

Nondeterminism and tokenizer quirks: batch-size/padding and fp differences move logprobs; leading-space handling (' A' vs 'A') flips MCQ scoring; detect by sanity-checking the random baseline and diffing against a reference implementation

notes.title: Snippet - Paired Bootstrap for Model Comparison
notes.scope: Runnable code that decides whether model A really beats model B on the same benchmark items, using a paired bootstrap plus the McNemar closed form. IN: the numpy implementation, inputs, and the expertise-bearing decisions. OUT: the conceptual statistics narrative (link to Statistical Rigor in Model Evaluation).
key_points: Inputs: two boolean arrays of per-item correctness over the SAME items for models A and B; output: bootstrap CI on the accuracy difference and the fraction of resamples favoring A
Method: resample item indices with replacement (10k iterations), recompute delta-accuracy each time, take the 2.5/97.5 percentiles; set a seed for reproducibility
Show McNemar's test as the closed-form paired alternative on the discordant-pairs count (b, c) for the same-items binary case
Why paired: the two models see identical items so their scores are correlated; the paired test removes shared-item variance and is far more powerful than comparing two independent marginal CIs
The load-bearing lesson in the comments: overlapping marginal confidence intervals do NOT imply a non-significant difference -- this is the single most common statistical error in model comparison
Note BCa vs percentile bootstrap tradeoff and why item-level resampling assumes independence (flag cluster bootstrap for MMLU-style subject structure)
Dependencies: numpy only, pure-Python fallback; expected output printed as 'delta = X, 95% CI [lo, hi], P(A>B) = p'
links: Concept - Statistical Rigor in Model Evaluation

notes.title: Concept - Membership Inference for Contamination Detection
notes.scope: The black-box and gray-box methods for detecting whether specific text was in a model's training data, and the open debate over whether they actually work. IN: the detection algorithms, their assumptions, and the reliability critique. OUT: the contamination phenomenon and canary discipline (link to Benchmark Contamination) and corpus dedup (owned by 05).
key_points: Min-K% Prob (Shi et al. 2023): average the log-probability of the k% least-likely tokens; seen text has fewer high-surprise tokens; Min-K%++ normalizes by the token's distribution for a stronger signal

Other detectors: perplexity/zlib ratio (from the Carlini et al. extraction line), DE-COP (Duarte et al. 2024) using multiple-choice paraphrase where a contaminated model prefers the verbatim option, guided prompting (Golchin & Surdeanu) asking the model to complete the next test item, and the Oren et al. 2023 exchangeability test on canonical benchmark ordering
Reliability critique: Duan et al. 2024 'Do Membership Inference Attacks Work on LLMs?' show many methods barely beat random in realistic settings; Maini et al. blind baselines expose the same problem
The core confound: 'member' and 'non-member' splits usually differ in date/topic/distribution, so detectors exploit temporal shift rather than true membership -- inflated reported AUCs
Where they do work: verbatim rare strings and long unique passages; where they fail: paraphrased, translated, or common-distribution data
Consequence: no reliable black-box contamination detector exists as of 2026; canary strings and strict release-date discipline remain the durable defenses
Connection to privacy: the same machinery underlies training-data extraction and privacy audits

notes.title: Concept - Meta-Evaluation of LLM Judges
notes.scope: How you validate the evaluator itself: measuring whether an LLM judge (or reward model) actually agrees with ground truth. IN: the meta-benchmarks, agreement metrics, adversarial findings, and the scalable-oversight frontier. OUT: applying a judge in practice (link to LLM-as-Judge and its Gotchas) and reward-model training (owned by 06).
key_points: The question: a judge's numbers are only as trustworthy as the judge, so you must evaluate the evaluator against human gold or verifiable answers

Meta-benchmarks: JudgeBench (Tan et al. 2024), RewardBench (Lambert et al. 2024, for reward models and judges), LLMBar (Zeng et al. 2023, adversarial instruction-following judging), plus MT-Bench/Arena human-agreement studies
Metrics: human-agreement rate, Cohen's kappa, Spearman correlation with human rankings, swap-consistency, and separability/discriminative power (can the judge tell close models apart?)

Findings: strong judges hit ~80% agreement with humans on easy preferences (near human-human ~81%) but collapse on adversarial and hard-reasoning items -- LLMBar shows judges fooled by confident, well-formatted wrong answers
Generation-verification gap: judging is often easier than generating, which is why weaker verifiers can still supervise stronger generators -- but this gap narrows or inverts on superhuman outputs

Optimization pressure closes the loop with Goodhart: once a judge becomes an optimization target (RLHF reward, best-of-n selection), its errors get exploited and it must be re-validated under pressure
Frontier: scalable oversight -- how to judge outputs that exceed human ability to verify (debate, recursive reward modeling, verifier training)
links: Concept - Goodhart's Law in Model Evaluation

notes.title: Concept - Private and Dynamic Benchmarks
notes.scope: Contamination-resistant evaluation via held-out, live, or procedurally generated benchmarks. IN: the mechanisms (private holdouts, date-windowing, templated generation, adversarial-in-the-loop), their tradeoffs, and the contamination-signal evidence. OUT: the contamination phenomenon (link to Benchmark Contamination) and Goodhart dynamics generally (link to Goodhart's Law).
key_points: Motivation: static public benchmarks saturate and get contaminated -- the 'eval crisis' -- so fresh or hidden test data is needed to keep measuring real capability

Private holdouts: Scale SEAL leaderboards, GPQA's protected portions, and ARC-AGI's private set (with prize) submit via API-only so the test never leaks -- at the cost of reproducibility and trust in the host

Live/updated: LiveBench (Aug 2024) refreshes monthly from recent sources; LiveCodeBench date-windows problems by release date so only post-cutoff items count -- and models measurably drop on post-cutoff problems, a direct contamination signal

Procedural/templated: GSM-Symbolic (Mirzadeh et al. / Apple 2024) generates variants by swapping names and numbers and shows accuracy drops and high variance when only surface details change; GSM1k rebuilds fresh grade-school problems
Adversarial-in-the-loop: DynaBench and Adversarial NLI collect human-written examples that fool current models, keeping the benchmark ahead of the models
Crowd Elo as ever-fresh: Chatbot Arena is effectively a living benchmark because prompts are novel and private
Tradeoffs: private sacrifices reproducibility, live sacrifices cross-time comparability, templated risks narrowness -- pick per the failure you most need to prevent

notes.title: Concept - Prompt Format Sensitivity in Evaluation
notes.scope: The tribal knowledge that trivial, semantically-equivalent formatting changes swing benchmark scores by many points at fixed model and data, and that a format favoring one model can flip the ranking against another. IN: the measured spreads, the sources, and the few-shot ordering effect. OUT: the token-level scoring machinery (link to Answer Scoring and Normalization) and MCQ position bias specifically (link to Multiple-Choice Symbol Binding).
key_points: FormatSpread (Sclar et al. 2023/2024, 'Quantifying Language Models' Sensitivity to Spurious Features in Prompt Design'): semantically-equivalent formats produce accuracy spreads up to ~76 points on some tasks, commonly 5-10+ points -- and the best format differs per model, so rankings flip on formatting alone
Sources: separator choice (':' vs ')' vs newline), casing of the 'Answer' cue, spacing, option delimiters, field ordering, and few-shot separators -- none of which change meaning

Few-shot ordering: Lu et al. 2022 'Fantastically Ordered Prompts' show exemplar order alone can move a model from near-random to near-SOTA; majority-label and recency biases in the shot set skew predictions
The 'prompt lottery': single-format evaluation is a coin flip, so leaderboard positions can be format artifacts rather than capability differences
Interaction with tokenization: whitespace and leading-space handling change the very logprobs being compared (ties into the scoring notes)

Practitioner remedies: report a distribution over formats (FormatSpread), evaluate under the model's own chat template, or fix one carefully-audited format and disclose it -- never quietly pick the format that flatters your model
Why unicorn: almost nobody reports format variance, yet it can dwarf the reported gap between two models
links: Concept - Multiple-Choice Symbol Binding and Position Bias

notes.title: Concept - Answer Scoring and Normalization
notes.scope: The arcana of turning a model's raw output into a benchmark score, where the choice of scoring method silently determines reported SOTA. IN: log-likelihood vs generation scoring, the normalization variants (acc, acc_norm, unconditional/PMI), and free-generation answer extraction. OUT: format-level variance (link to Prompt Format Sensitivity) and MCQ position/symbol bias (link to Multiple-Choice Symbol Binding).
key_points: Two regimes: log-likelihood/cloze scoring (compare P(completion) across options, used for MMLU/HellaSwag) vs generation-and-parse (let the model produce text, then extract the answer) -- they can rank models differently and must not be mixed in a comparison

acc vs acc_norm: acc uses raw option log-likelihood; acc_norm normalizes by completion length (lm-eval uses byte length) to correct the bias toward shorter options -- the two can differ 5-10 points and reorder models on HellaSwag and ARC

Surface-form competition (Holtzman et al. 2021): raw probability penalizes valid answers that happen to be rarer token strings ('computer' beats 'PC'); PMI/unconditional normalization divides by P(answer) alone to fix it

Letter vs full-answer scoring: scoring the option letter 'A' vs scoring the full answer text gives different rankings, and weak models may know the answer but fail to emit the letter (ties to symbol binding)
Byte-length vs token-length normalization: which one the original paper used changes the number, so 'acc_norm' is not a single well-defined quantity across harnesses

Free-generation math grading: answer extraction (\boxed{} parsing) and equivalence checking (sympy for MATH) produce false negatives on equivalent forms (1/2 vs 0.5, unsimplified expressions) and false positives on lucky substring matches
Why unicorn: these choices decide which model is 'SOTA', yet only harness maintainers usually understand them -- the Open LLM Leaderboard's deliberate acc_norm choices are a concrete example
links: Concept - Multiple-Choice Symbol Binding and Position Bias

notes.title: Concept - Multiple-Choice Symbol Binding and Position Bias
notes.scope: Why multiple-choice scores are confounded by which symbol (A/B/C/D) and position an answer sits at, independent of content, and why letter-scoring is not the same as knowing the answer. IN: the selection-bias evidence, symbol-binding failure, mechanisms, and debiasing. OUT: general scoring-method choices (link to Answer Scoring and Normalization) and harness plumbing (link to Designing an Eval Harness).
key_points: Selection bias: Zheng et al. 2023 'Large Language Models Are Not Robust Multiple Choice Selectors' show models have inherent priors toward specific option IDs; permuting option order changes accuracy by up to ~20+ points, and they propose PriDe to estimate and subtract the positional prior

Symbol binding (MCSB): Robinson et al. 2022 -- whether a model can reliably associate a letter with its option; weaker models fail to output the correct letter even when they 'know' the answer, so letter-scoring understates their knowledge

Mechanisms: token-level priors on ' A' vs ' B', positional bias inherited from pretraining formats, and few-shot answer-distribution skew (if the shots' answers cluster on one letter, the model over-predicts it)
Frontier vs small models: GPT-4/Claude-class models are less affected but still measurably biased; small models are heavily biased -- so the confound interacts with the model being ranked
Debiasing: cyclic-permutation averaging (score all rotations of the options), PriDe calibration, balanced few-shot answer distributions, or scoring full-answer log-likelihood instead of the letter
Consequence: this is a major reason MMLU numbers are irreproducible across harnesses and why 'letter accuracy' is a biased proxy for knowledge
Why unicorn: it explains a whole class of contradictory leaderboard results that most practitioners attribute to the model rather than the scoring format

notes.title: Lore - Benchmark Scandals
notes.scope: The war stories where benchmark numbers turned out to be marketing: fraud, contamination, implementation discrepancies, and cherry-picking. IN: the narratives with honest evidence-status labels and the mechanical lesson each teaches. OUT: the underlying mechanisms (link to Benchmark Contamination and Goodhart's Law) which these stories illustrate.
key_points: Reflection-70B (Sept 2024, Matt Shumer/HyperWrite): claimed SOTA via 'reflection tuning'; independent evaluators (Artificial Analysis and others) could not reproduce it and found the API appeared to proxy to Claude/GPT -- evidence status: well-documented fiasco, widely judged fraud

GSM1k (Zhang et al. 2024): rebuilding GSM8K-style problems fresh exposed 8-13% drops for several families (worst on some Mistral/Phi checkpoints) while frontier models held -- evidence status: peer-reviewed, quantified overfit

Open LLM Leaderboard MMLU discrepancy (2023): HuggingFace, the original code, and HELM produced different MMLU numbers for the same model; HF's 'What's going on with the Open LLM Leaderboard' post dissected it -- evidence status: verified, documented by the maintainers
AlpacaEval length gaming: win-rate was inflated by output length until the length-controlled version shipped -- evidence status: verified, fixed by the authors
Vendor cherry-picking: launch charts comparing a model's cons@64 or maj@k against competitors' pass@1, or hand-picked subsets -- evidence status: recurring pattern, apples-to-oranges by construction

The Leaderboard Illusion (Singh et al. 2025): allegations of private multi-variant testing and selective disclosure on Chatbot Arena favoring large labs -- evidence status: disputed, one detailed paper plus rebuttals
The lesson, stated mechanically: a benchmark number without a pinned harness, decontamination, confidence intervals, and apples-to-apples comparison is a marketing artifact, not a measurement
